Emu named Eric stalks pensioner in Queensland suburb

02 Nov 2026, 10:33 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily World Desk · Source: www.abc.net.au

2 min read

Key takeawaysThe situation remains unresolved; Richards continues to encounter Eric daily, and no agency has taken formal action to relocate the bird.

Image: www.abc.net.au · Photo source · Resized and letterboxed to 16:9; no AI generation

In this article
  1. The problem
  2. Reported incidents (as told to ABC News)
  3. Official response
  4. Wildlife expert view
  5. Practical steps for residents

The problem

  • Since early 2025, pensioner Mal Richards of Bluewater, a suburb on Townsville’s outskirts, has reported that an emu he calls Eric follows him around his yard and driveway every morning before 6 a.m.
  • Richards says the bird blocks his path, honks loudly, and leaves droppings on his driveway, making routine chores feel unsafe.

Reported incidents (as told to ABC News)

  • Daily harassment – Richards claims the emu “stands around honking all day” and appears whenever he turns to do a task.
  • Physical risk – He worries about the emu’s powerful kick and large feet, noting, “I’m a pensioner, right?”
  • Community sightings – The local Bluewater Facebook page is filled with photos and warnings for drivers, and a resident reported schoolchildren having to climb a fence to avoid the bird.

Official response

  • The Townsville City Council and the Queensland Department of Primary Industries have been contacted, but officials say the animal “has not been seen to exhibit any concerning behaviour.”
  • A spokesperson for the Department of Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation advised residents to give the emu space, avoid feeding it, and not provide easy access to food.
  • Local council regulations allow an emu to be kept on a property larger than 2,000 m² if an adequate enclosure is provided; no law currently forces removal.

Wildlife expert view

  • Jackie Hasling, a wildlife educator, says Eric is likely a former pet and therefore less aggressive than wild emus. She recommends:
  • Back away slowly if the bird approaches.
  • Hold a rake or stick to appear taller.
  • Use a tree or other barrier between you and the bird.
  • Accept that droppings are an inevitable nuisance.

Practical steps for residents

  • Secure fencing – Ensure any gaps are closed; emus can squeeze through surprisingly small openings.
  • No feeding – Removing food sources reduces the bird’s incentive to linger.
  • Report to wildlife officers – If the emu shows truly threatening behaviour, document the incident (date, time, photos) and contact the state wildlife rangers.
  • Neighbourly cooperation – Share sightings on community pages to help authorities gauge the bird’s range.

*The situation remains unresolved; Richards continues to encounter Eric daily, and no agency has taken formal action to relocate the bird.*
